name: Large-Scale Compute on Institutional Data
title: Large-Scale Compute on Institutional Data
answer: Large-scale compute on institutional data covers the use of distributed and high performance computing to analyze datasets held by universities, hospitals, government agencies and corporations. The work spans quantitative modeling, simulation, statistical analysis and machine learning on data that is often too large or too sensitive to move to a single workstation. Reproducibility is a core requirement, so the scope includes versioning of code, data and compute environments. Institutional data may include administrative records, research measurements, clinical information and operational logs.

sections.body: Large-scale compute on institutional data covers the use of distributed and high performance computing to analyze datasets held by universities, hospitals, government agencies and corporations. The work spans quantitative modeling, simulation, statistical analysis and machine learning on data that is often too large or too sensitive to move to a single workstation. Reproducibility is a core requirement, so the scope includes versioning of code, data and compute environments. Institutional data may include administrative records, research measurements, clinical information and operational logs.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: This work runs on institutional high performance computing clusters, cloud platforms and hybrid systems that combine on premises and rented capacity. Typical components include CPU and GPU nodes, parallel file systems, high speed interconnects, job schedulers such as Slurm, and container runtimes. Reproducible setups often add workflow managers, environment managers and artifact stores so that a run can be repeated with the same software stack. Storage is usually tiered, with fast scratch space for active jobs and slower object or tape storage for long term retention.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done by first ingesting and cleaning institutional data, then recording its schema and provenance before analysis. Analysts write parallel or distributed jobs that split computation across many nodes, often using frameworks for batch processing, array jobs or message passing. Model training and statistical fitting are logged with hyperparameters, random seeds and data versions. Results are validated against held out data or prior findings, and the full pipeline is packaged in containers or workflow definitions so another researcher can rerun it.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk center on who may access institutional data and for what purpose, governed by data use agreements, institutional review boards and internal access controls. Sensitive records are typically de-identified or pseudonymized before compute jobs run, and audit logs track which user ran which job on which dataset. Provenance systems record the lineage of every derived table, model and figure back to the original source files. Risks include re-identification, unauthorized copying, and silent changes to data or code that break reproducibility.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward federated and distributed analysis that keeps raw institutional data in place while sharing only model updates or summary statistics. Confidential computing and hardware based enclaves are being explored to let institutions run shared workloads on sensitive data with stronger isolation. Reproducibility is becoming more automated through provenance capture at the scheduler and filesystem level. Energy efficiency and carbon accounting are also becoming part of how large scale institutional compute is planned and reported.
